cards.title: What Is a Value Object?
cards.teaser: A value object is a domain concept whose identity is entirely defined by its attributes — two instances with the same attributes are the same thing, with no need to distinguish them by memory address or a database row ID.

runs.text: Eric Evans introduced the value object in the Blue Book (Domain-Driven Design, 2003, Chapter 5) alongside the entity as one of the two primary building blocks of a domain model. The key distinction is identity:

items.text: — has a unique identity that persists through the lifetime of the object. Two Customer objects with the same name are still different customers if their IDs differ.
— has no meaningful identity beyond its attributes. Two Money objects both representing $50.00 USD are completely interchangeable. No ID is needed or meaningful.

runs.text: Evans writes: "An object that represents a descriptive aspect of the domain with no conceptual identity is called a Value Object." The test is simple: if you replaced one instance with another bearing identical attributes and no code could tell the difference, it is a value object.
Classic examples:
Money
(amount + currency),
Color
(RGB triple),
DateRange
(start + end date),
Coordinate
(latitude + longitude). In each case, swapping two instances with equal attributes causes no observable change.

Value objects are described in Evans's Blue Book, Chapter 5 ("A Model Expressed in Software"), alongside Entities and Services. The chapter is foundational: it establishes that most domain concepts do not need identity and that treating them as entities is a modeling mistake with real implementation costs.
A value object is a domain concept where the data is the identity — two objects with the same values are the same thing, period. You do not need to track which specific instance you are holding.

cards.title: Immutability — VOs Never Change
cards.teaser: A value object must be immutable: once constructed, its attributes cannot change. Any operation that would logically 'modify' a VO instead returns a new VO — the original is unchanged. This property is what makes VOs safe to share freely.

runs.text: Immutability is not optional for value objects — it is their defining safety property. A mutable VO destroys the equality-by-value guarantee because mutating one reference to a shared VO silently changes all aliases to it.
The canonical immutable pattern returns a new instance on transformation:
Python's
@dataclass(frozen=True)
enforces immutability at runtime. Java records and Kotlin data classes with
val
properties provide the same guarantee. In languages without structural enforcement, discipline and code review must compensate.

Immutability unlocks a set of engineering benefits beyond correctness: VOs are safe to use as dictionary keys, safe to cache, safe to share across threads, and safe to pass to any function without defensive copying.

A common mistake is storing a mutable collection inside a VO and calling the outer object immutable. If Money held a mutable list of applied discounts, callers could modify that list and violate immutability. All internal fields must also be immutable for the VO to be truly immutable.

A value object never changes in place. Adding tax to a price returns a new price — it does not modify the original. Immutability is what makes it safe to pass a VO around freely without worrying about unintended side effects.

cards.title: Side-Effect-Free Behavior
cards.teaser: VO methods are pure functions: given the same inputs they return the same outputs and modify nothing outside their own scope. This makes them trivially testable, safe to call speculatively, and easy to reason about in complex domain logic.

runs.text: Evans describes value objects as having "side-effect-free functions" — methods that query or transform the VO but never modify global or external state. Combined with immutability, this makes VOs the safest objects in the entire domain model.
A side-effect-free VO method:

items.text: Takes only its own fields and explicit arguments as inputs.
Returns a new VO or a primitive result.
Never writes to a database, sends an HTTP request, logs to a file, or modifies any shared mutable state.
Produces the exact same output for the same inputs every time — referential transparency.

runs.text: The practical payoff is enormous. Pure VO methods can be tested with a single assertion and no mocking. They can be called in any order. They can be parallelized. They can be evaluated lazily. A domain model whose business logic is expressed as VO transformations is dramatically easier to maintain than one where methods reach out to databases or services mid-calculation.

If a method on a VO needs to call an external service, that is a strong signal that the method does not belong on the VO — it belongs on a domain service or an application service that coordinates the VO with infrastructure.

Side-effect-free means VO methods are like math functions: same inputs always give the same output, and nothing in the world changes when you call them. They are the easiest code to test and reason about.

cards.title: Self-Validation — Always Valid
cards.teaser: A value object enforces its own invariants in the constructor. An invalid VO cannot exist — construction either succeeds with a valid object or raises an exception. The domain model is protected from invalid state from the moment of creation.

runs.text: One of the most important properties of a value object is that it is always in a valid state. The constructor is the single entry point, and it validates all invariants before the object comes into existence. There is no two-step construction, no "call validate() after you set the properties" pattern.
Self-validation eliminates an entire class of defensive programming. If your
Order
entity holds an
Email
VO rather than a raw string, you never need to re-validate the email inside
Order
or in any service that receives it. The type itself is proof of validity.
This is the principle of making illegal states unrepresentable. A
str
can hold any sequence of characters. An
Email
VO can only hold a structurally valid email address. The difference is enforced by the type system.

Self-validation applies not just to format ("is this a valid email structure?") but to domain rules ("is this a positive money amount?", "does this date range have an end after the start?"). Anything that must be true for the value to be meaningful should be enforced in the constructor.
A VO validates itself when it is created — if the data is invalid, construction fails immediately. Once you have a VO in hand, you know it is valid and you never need to check again.

cards.title: Primitive Obsession
cards.teaser: Primitive obsession is using raw strings, ints, and floats to represent domain concepts instead of dedicated types. It is the most common anti-pattern that value objects cure — and it causes subtle bugs that type-checking cannot catch.

runs.text: Primitive obsession occurs when the codebase uses language primitives —
str
int
float
— for domain concepts that have their own semantics, constraints, and behavior. The surface looks fine; the failures are subtle and delayed.
A canonical example — a function that processes a money transfer using raw primitives:

Primitive obsession also scatters validation. If email addresses are stored as strings, every function that accepts an email must re-validate or trust the caller. Validation logic duplicates across the codebase and inevitably diverges.

items.text: Common primitives that deserve VO promotion:
user ID, product SKU, email address, phone number, postal code, currency amount, latitude/longitude, ISO country code, version number.

runs.text: The worst form of primitive obsession is using a plain int for multiple distinct domain identifiers in the same function — order ID, customer ID, product ID. Static analysis cannot distinguish them, and a one-character transposition in argument order becomes a silent production bug.

Primitive obsession is using a plain string or int when you should use a richer type — like using a raw number for both price and quantity, which lets you accidentally multiply a price by another price. Value objects give each concept its own type with its own rules.

cards.title: The Money Pattern
cards.teaser: Martin Fowler's Money pattern is the canonical value object example: amount and currency are inseparable, arithmetic must handle currency matching, and floating-point must be avoided. Money appears in nearly every business domain and gets it wrong in nearly every codebase.

runs.text: Martin Fowler introduced the Money pattern in
Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture
(2002) and it remains the most instructive VO example because it captures every VO property in one concept.
Key design decisions encoded in this VO:

items.text: in IEEE 754. Using cents as integers avoids rounding drift entirely.
of 1000 is ambiguous. USD 10.00 is unambiguous.
— adding USD and EUR requires an exchange service, which is infrastructure. The VO correctly refuses to silently convert.

runs.text: The Money pattern shows why value objects exist: an amount alone is meaningless without a currency, the two must travel together, and arithmetic between different currencies needs an external service to resolve. Encoding those rules in one immutable object eliminates an entire category of bugs.

cards.title: Common Value Object Types
cards.teaser: Email, PhoneNumber, Address, DateRange, Quantity, PostalCode, Coordinate, Percentage, and URL are the recurring value objects that appear across almost every business domain. Each wraps a primitive and adds validation, formatting, and behavior.

runs.text: Most business domains share a vocabulary of common value objects. Recognizing them on contact avoids rebuilding the same logic in every project.

runs.text: Each of these wraps a raw string or number and converts it into a domain-meaningful type with enforced invariants. The pattern is always the same: validate in the constructor, expose domain-relevant behavior, store in the most precise normalized form.

Email, PhoneNumber, DateRange, and Money are the "usual suspects" of value objects — they appear in almost every domain because every business deals with contact info, time ranges, and money. Building them once with proper validation saves rebuilding the same logic in dozens of places.

cards.title: VO Composition — VOs Inside VOs
cards.teaser: Value objects can contain other value objects, creating rich composite types that model domain concepts precisely. An Address VO that holds a PostalCode VO gets the postal code's validation for free and composes it into a larger whole.

runs.text: Composition is the natural consequence of VOs being immutable value types. Because there is no identity to track, a VO can be freely embedded inside another VO. The outer VO's equality follows from the equality of all its fields, including any nested VOs.
The embedded
PostalCode
VO carries its own validation.
Address

does not need to repeat postal code logic — it inherits it through composition. If the postal code format changes (adding new country rules), the change propagates automatically to every VO that embeds
PostalCode

VO composition follows the same principle as function composition: complex behavior from simple, well-defined parts. The outer VO trusts its inner VOs to be valid. Validation responsibility is distributed to where the domain concept lives, not centralized in a god-object validator.

You can build VOs from other VOs — an Address can hold a PostalCode VO, which knows its own format rules. The outer object gets all that validation for free, and equality cascades through every nested field automatically.

cards.title: Equality Semantics — All Fields, Not Identity
cards.teaser: Value objects implement structural equality: two VOs are equal if and only if all their attributes are equal. This must be implemented explicitly in languages that default to reference equality, and it is the foundational contract everything else depends on.

runs.text: Most object-oriented languages default to reference (identity) equality for class instances:
a == b
is true only if
a
and
b
are the same object in memory. For VOs, this is wrong — two distinct
Money(500, 'USD')
instances must be equal.

items.text: . Legacy classes must override both by hand — and must keep them consistent (same fields in both methods).
over all constructor properties. Only properties in the constructor (not in the body) participate — a subtle gotcha.
types generate structural equality over all properties.

runs.text: A critical invariant: if
a.equals(b)
is true, then
a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()
must also be true. Violating this breaks hash maps, sets, and any data structure that uses hashing. Manually implementing
equals()
without
hashCode()
is a common defect in Java VO implementations.

VOs use value equality, not reference equality — two separate Money objects both holding $50 USD must compare as equal. In most languages you have to implement this explicitly; modern record/dataclass features generate it for you.

cards.title: Hashability — VOs as Map Keys
cards.teaser: Because VOs have structural equality and never change, they are ideal map and set keys. A DateRange key, a Money key, a Coordinate key — all are natural uses that primitives cannot provide safely. Hashability is immutability's reward.

runs.text: A hashable object can be used as a dictionary key or placed in a set. For a VO, hashability follows directly from two properties that VOs already have: structural equality and immutability.

items.text: — the hash must be consistent with equality. Two equal VOs must have the same hash.
— a mutable object used as a dict key becomes unreachable if its hash changes after insertion. Immutable VOs guarantee the hash never changes.

runs.text: Practical uses of VOs as map keys:
Without VO hashability you would use tuple keys —
('USD', 'EUR')
— which are untyped, unvalidated, and can be accidentally compared with other tuples of the same shape. VO keys are self-documenting and validated.

Because VOs are immutable and use value equality, they work perfectly as dictionary keys or set members. Their hash never changes, and two equal VOs produce the same hash — both required for correct behavior in hash-based data structures.

cards.title: Persisting Value Objects
cards.teaser: ORMs and databases offer two persistence strategies for VOs: embed them directly in the owning entity's table (preferred), or give them their own table. The embedded strategy preserves the VO's conceptual unity; the separate-table strategy trades simplicity for queryability.

runs.text: Persisting value objects requires a mapping decision that ORMs handle differently. The two primary strategies:

items.text: — the VO's fields become columns in the owner's table. A
table. No join required; data is co-located with its owner. This is the preferred default.
— the VO gets its own table with a foreign key back to the owner. Useful when the VO is large, queried independently, or shared by multiple entities. Costs an extra join per load.

runs.text: ORM-specific patterns:

runs.text: Never give a VO its own surrogate key in the database unless forced by a legacy schema. A synthetic ID column on a VO table creates an entity-like persistence model that tempts code to load VOs by ID — violating the VO's statelessness. If you find yourself loading a VO by ID, it is probably an entity.

VOs are most naturally stored as extra columns in their owner's table — a Money VO on an Order becomes two columns, amount and currency, in the orders table. This avoids a join, keeps the data together, and mirrors the domain model directly.

cards.title: VO vs Entity — When to Upgrade
cards.teaser: A concept that starts as a VO can become an entity if the business starts tracking it individually over time. The trigger is identity: when the domain needs to distinguish two instances with the same attributes, or track history independently, the VO has become an entity.

runs.text: The VO vs entity decision is not a permanent classification — it is a modeling choice that should be revisited as the domain evolves. Evans is explicit: the same concept may be a VO in one context and an entity in another.
Signals that a VO should be promoted to an entity:

items.text: The business needs to track individual instances.

Two banknotes of $50 are interchangeable as Money VOs. But in a cash management system where banknotes have serial numbers and are individually tracked (stolen bills, currency destruction), each note is an entity.
The business needs a history or audit log.
An Email address used as a VO in a single-profile system becomes an entity in a marketing system that tracks when addresses were added, verified, bounced, or unsubscribed.
The concept has its own lifecycle.
If an Address can be "created," "verified," "marked invalid," and "archived" independently of any customer, it has a lifecycle and needs identity.
The concept is shared by multiple owners.
If multiple Customer entities share the same legal Address and changes to one should not cascade to the others, you need identity to distinguish the shared reference from a copy.

runs.text: The converse also applies: an entity can be simplified to a VO when identity turns out not to matter. Many codebases over-eagerly assign database IDs to everything; auditing the model often reveals concepts that would be clearer as VOs.

Evans's heuristic from the Blue Book: start with VO, promote to entity only when the domain requires it. Entities are heavier — they need identity management, lifecycle handling, and often more complex repository logic. VOs are cheaper and should be preferred when they model the domain accurately.

A VO becomes an entity when the business needs to tell two instances with the same attributes apart — when two $50 bills are not interchangeable because one has a tracked serial number. Identity is the signal to upgrade.

cards.title: Refactoring to Value Objects
cards.teaser: Extracting VOs from scattered primitive parameters is one of the highest-ROI refactorings in a DDD codebase. The pattern is: find a cluster of primitives that always travel together, extract a VO, move validation and behavior into it, and update call sites.

runs.text: Primitive clusters — groups of primitives that consistently appear together in function signatures, data classes, or entity fields — are the strongest signal that a VO should be extracted. The refactoring has a repeatable pattern.
Before — primitive cluster scattered across the call stack:
The refactoring steps:

items.text: — look for 2–4 parameters that always appear together in the same order.
— if the domain experts have a name for the combination, use it. Money, Coordinate, DateRange.
— create an immutable class with those fields and move validation into its constructor.
— move methods that only use those fields into the VO.
— replace the parameter cluster with the VO throughout the codebase.

runs.text: When you see the same two or three parameters always passing together, that cluster is usually a VO trying to escape. Extract them into a class, move the validation in, and every function that accepts the VO gets the validation for free.

cards.title: Wrapping Identifiers — The ID Value Object
cards.teaser: Wrapping raw IDs in a lightweight VO — UserId, OrderId, ProductId — eliminates argument-order bugs, makes function signatures self-documenting, and enables type-safe ULID or UUID generation. The cost is near zero; the benefit is permanent.

runs.text: One underused application of VOs is wrapping entity identifiers. Most codebases pass entity IDs as raw ints or strings, creating a class of bugs that is invisible to the type checker and silent at runtime.
The ULID (Universally Unique Lexicographically Sortable Identifier) format is a popular alternative to UUID for database IDs: 128-bit, URL-safe, lexicographically sortable by generation time. A
UserId
VO can enforce ULID format on construction exactly as
Email
enforces email format, making the type self-validating.
This pattern pairs naturally with the repository pattern: repositories accept typed ID VOs rather than raw primitives, making the query contract explicit.

Wrap your entity IDs in tiny VO types — UserId, OrderId, ProductId. The cost is almost nothing, but passing an OrderId where a UserId is expected becomes a compile-time error instead of a silent production bug.

cards.title: Value Objects in Context — Bounded Context Boundaries
cards.teaser: The same concept can be a different VO in different bounded contexts — and that is correct. Money in the billing context carries tax metadata; Money in the reporting context is a simple number. Translation at context boundaries is normal DDD practice.

runs.text: Bounded contexts, covered in Chapter 2, apply directly to VO design. The same domain word can refer to a different structure, different invariants, and different behavior in each context. VOs are context-local types, not global shared types.
A worked example across two contexts:

items.text: . Tax details are irrelevant; the reporting engine needs totals.

runs.text: These are genuinely different types. They should not share a class just because they carry the same word in the ubiquitous language of their respective contexts. A translator at the context boundary converts billing's
Money
to reporting's
Money
by discarding irrelevant fields.

The anti-pattern is a single "universal" Money VO with optional fields that different contexts populate differently. Optional fields on a VO signal that the concept is being stretched across contexts it was not designed for — the VO's self-validation cannot be complete if some fields are optional for structural reasons rather than domain reasons.

Evans explicitly allows (and recommends) that the same domain word refers to different model elements in different bounded contexts. The ubiquitous language is bounded — "Money" in billing is not the same concept as "Money" in reporting, even though both use the word. VOs are inexpensive enough to duplicate across context boundaries.

The same word can mean different things in different bounded contexts, and that is fine. A Money VO in billing carries tax details; in reporting it is just a number with a currency. Define the VO for the context it lives in, translate at the boundary, and do not force a single universal VO to serve both.
